text:
Disney+’s new Korean original series "The Remarried Empress" features Korean actors addressing one another with Western names while navigating a fictional European-style empire in elaborate gowns and military uniforms.
When the initial teaser trailers were released, some viewers expressed skepticism, comparing the visual aesthetic to a cosplay convention. However, upon its official premiere on Nov. 3, the series completely shattered expectations. Within just three days of release, the drama officially became the most-watched Disney+ local original series of all time worldwide, based on cumulative global views.
Audience feedback across global fan platforms has mirrored this enthusiasm. Viewers who binged the first four episodes highlighted its "slow, subtle, addictive royal drama vibe." Fans on Reddit praised the adaptation as "visually stunning" with a "fairytale-like feel," admitting that while anyone expecting a literal live-action translation of the webtoon might be surprised, it remains deeply rewarding as a "K-drama in its own right." Ultimately, audiences voiced genuine appreciation for creating "something we don't usually get to see."
Based on the wildly popular web novel and webtoon of the same name, "The Remarried Empress" follows Navier (Shin Min-a), the perfect empress of the Eastern Empire. When her husband, Emperor Sovieshu (Ju Ji-hoon), demands a divorce to elevate his mistress, Navier accepts — on the condition that she be granted approval to remarry Heinrey (Lee Jong-suk), prince of the Western Kingdom.
The show quickly dominated international streaming charts. According to global tracking data, "The Remarried Empress" surged to No. 1 in 33 countries and regions while soaring to No. 2 overall on Disney+’s global TV rankings, standing right behind Marvel's "Vision Quest." Domestically and regionally, it locked down the top spot in Korea, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan, while sweeping weekly Korean drama buzzworthiness rankings.
To capitalize on the show's immersive world-building, Disney+ recently opened an interactive pop-up store in Seongsu-dong, Seongdong District, Seoul. Running until Sunday, visitors are greeted as "Lady" or "Lord" and given custom nobility titles, inviting fans directly into the romance fantasy universe.
At the entrance, visitors provide their information to receive custom imperial guest badges with a world-appropriate name and country of origin. Inside, attendees explore meticulously recreated sets of Empress Navier’s private quarters, including her bedroom and writing suite. The pop-up also showcases actual dresses and accessories worn by Shin Min-a, bringing the webtoon's grand mise-en-scène into reality. In an interactive photo booth, visitors sit on a royal throne as half a dozen attendants shower them with theatrical compliments.
"I stumbled upon the pop-up while walking by and waited about 10 minutes to get in," said Kim Bo-mi, a 21-year-old university student. "I had only watched short clips of the show before, but feeling like an empress in real life was so much fun. Sitting on the throne while butler staff fawned over me was a bit embarrassing, but being treated like 'Lady Dravea' for a day made me really want to watch the full series."
A K-content creator in her late 30s shared her experience on social media. "The staff were so sweet — my heart completely melted. They engaged in playful small talk and kept telling me how beautiful I looked, which made the experience unforgettable," she said.
Culture critic Jung Duk-hyun highlighted the show's daring genre expansion.
"There is a surprisingly addictive pull to the show. While the core story follows familiar romance-fantasy tropes, the unfamiliar European setting — complete with grand palaces, lavish balls and high-society political intrigue — becomes remarkably refreshing when portrayed by Korean actors," he said.
"Even in an era where fantasy elements are widely accepted, K-dramas are still traditionally expected to ground themselves in reality. Portraying a Western-style romance where characters casually transform into birds is a provocative leap. Yet, this gamble works because of its high execution quality," Jung explained.
"Despite the initial unfamiliarity, the lavish set design, costume direction,\ and subdued, grounded directing style prevent the fantasy from feeling floaty. Anchored by heavy, stable performances from Ju and Shin, alongside striking visual fits from Lee Jong-suk and Lee Se-young, the show lands its ambitious vision."
